Wait until a well-known resident gives a speech at city hall.
questions.explanation: The board gives agreement a visible repeated act. Close neighbors can start it, nearby blocks can copy it, and the Friday rhythm beats another message or a leader-centered speech.

questions.prompt: A school garden has many quiet supporters, but workdays keep failing. Parents say they care, then no one signs up. Which design uses social habits best?
choices: Send a guilt email naming how much the children need the garden.
Have two friend groups claim the first beds, then post a weekly bed map where other families can add names.
Ask the principal to announce that gardening is now expected.
questions.explanation: The bed map turns caring into a visible role. Friend groups lower the risk of starting, and other families can see where to join. Guilt and top-down announcements lack a repeatable act.

questions.prompt: A tenants' group relies on one charismatic resident to call the landlord after every leak. Repairs stall whenever she is away. What is the weak point?
choices: The resident is not persuasive enough.
The landlord needs a more emotional story.
The action depends on one person instead of a visible routine others are expected to repeat.
questions.explanation: A movement cannot rest on one caller. The missing piece is a shared repair log, floor role, or repeated reporting routine that neighbors can carry without the same leader present.

questions.prompt: A volunteer clinic wants more translators at Saturday intake. The coordinator has three trusted translators and many loose contacts from partner groups. What should she build?
choices: A visible Saturday slot board started by the three trusted translators and shared with partner groups.
A private spreadsheet that only the coordinator can edit.
A social post saying translation is an important form of service.
questions.explanation: The trusted translators can launch the board, and partner groups can see open roles. The private spreadsheet hides participation, while a post names the value without creating a routine.

questions.prompt: A cycling club wants riders to report dangerous potholes. A viral photo gets attention for two days, then reports stop. Which change would make the action more durable?
choices: Ask the best rider to post more often.
Create a Sunday route card where pairs mark hazards and hand the card to the next group.
Tell riders that failing to report potholes is selfish.
questions.explanation: The route card creates a repeated handoff between riders. The viral photo had attention but no durable role; more posts or blame do not build peer expectation.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood pantry has a strong core team, but nobody outside their friend circle restocks shelves. What should the core team add?
choices: A closed chat where the core team can coordinate faster.
A speech thanking the core team for its dedication.
A public shelf card showing which block stocked each day and which block is next.
questions.explanation: The core team is strong-tie launch work, but scaling needs weak-tie visibility. A public shelf card gives other blocks a clear role; closed chat and thanks keep the work inside the same circle.

questions.prompt: A campus accessibility group has a list of students who privately support captioned events. Which plan best turns support into participation?
choices: Have two close student groups caption their first events, then post a visible event checklist other clubs can copy.
Keep the supporter list private and hope event planners ask for it.
Ask one popular professor to give a talk on inclusion.
questions.explanation: The first student groups make the act less lonely, and the checklist lets weaker ties copy the norm. A hidden list and a talk do not make captioning a repeated visible role.

questions.prompt: A library friends group wants residents to defend evening hours. Private support is high, but public comments are sparse. What question should guide the plan?
choices: Who can write the most moving statement?
Which visible weekly act lets close supporters start and casual users see they are expected to join?
How can the group make dissenters feel embarrassed?
questions.explanation: The guiding question looks for strong-tie launch, weak-tie spread, and a repeatable public role. Moving statements may help, but they do not by themselves create participation.

questions.prompt: A river cleanup organizer says, "Everyone cares, so the turnout will take care of itself." What is missing from that plan?
choices: A more dramatic photo of the polluted river.
A stronger statement that caring is morally required.
A visible routine for showing up, such as teams claiming weekly bags and signing the drop-off sheet.
questions.explanation: Caring is private until it has a role. Weekly bag claims and a drop-off sheet make participation visible and repeatable; photos and moral statements can spark attention without carrying action.

reviewCards.front: A cause has private support but no turnout. What is the first design question?
reviewCards.back: Ask what visible repeated act would let supporters show up. Private agreement needs a role, place, and rhythm before it can become collective action.

reviewCards.front: Why start a movement routine with strong ties?
reviewCards.back: Close ties make early participation less lonely and less risky. A small trusted group can model the act before weaker ties are asked to copy it.

reviewCards.front: What do weak ties add after close friends start acting?
reviewCards.back: Weak ties carry the behavior beyond the first circle. They let people who are not intimate friends see the act, recognize the norm, and join without a private invitation.

reviewCards.front: A campaign depends on one persuasive person. What risk should you see?
reviewCards.back: The action may stop when that person is absent. Build a shared ledger, board, card, or handoff so participation belongs to the group rather than one voice.

reviewCards.front: How do peer expectations become useful instead of vague pressure?
reviewCards.back: They become useful when tied to a concrete role people can see each other keeping: signing, pinning, clearing, claiming, carrying, or handing off on a repeated schedule.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is turning private support into a visible participation routine. Start with close ties who will act first, build a bridge for weaker ties to see and copy, and make the act repeat on a schedule. Do not count agreement as action until people have a role they can keep in public.

ifThenPlans.plan: If people say they support a cause but do not show up, then I will name one visible weekly act and ask two close-tie supporters to do it first.
If the first circle is acting but others are not, then I will place the role on a shared board, map, sheet, or calendar where weak ties already pass by.
If one person is carrying the action, then I will turn their task into a repeatable handoff that at least three people can perform without a speech.
If outrage is dropping after the first event, then I will schedule the next visible act before asking for more statements or posts.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one cause people near you privately support. Write one strong-tie starter, one weak-tie bridge, and one visible weekly act with a place, time, and role.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, look at one group effort you care about and ask whether it has all three layers: close-tie launch, weak-tie spread, and a visible repeated act.

memorableLines.text: A movement starts to move when agreement gets a place to stand.
memorableLines.why: It turns private support into a physical, repeatable image.

memorableLines.text: Strong ties light the first match; weak ties carry the flame across the room.
memorableLines.why: It separates launch work from scaling work in one memorable contrast.

memorableLines.text: Peer expectation works when it becomes a visible role people can see each other keeping.
memorableLines.why: It keeps social pressure grounded in a concrete action rather than abstract belonging.

chapters.title: The Neurology of Free Will
chapters.hook: The sleep-clinic note lies beside the hotel key, and the old mystery now has a door wedge.
chapters.counterintuition: A weak habit explanation begs for blanket pardon even though the strong form names the moment the loop became foreseeable. Devika asks that question first, then contains, redesigns, or avoids the cue before the next exposure repeats the harm.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one loop that could hurt someone if repeated. Write the cue, the likely harm, and the containment you would put in place before that cue appears again.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Automatic routines complicate responsibility, but once a risky loop is known and foreseeable, accountability returns as a duty to contain, redesign, or avoid it.

breakdown.fastRead:
A folded sleep-clinic note rests beside a hotel key packet. The first hallway incident felt mysterious. The second one was documented. At check-in, the traveler can still feel ashamed, but the loop is no longer unknowable.

That is where responsibility re-enters. Habit can explain why the body moves before clear choice appears. It does not erase the duty to manage a known risk.

Once the loop is visible, you no longer get to call it mysterious. Ask for the door-alarm wedge. Ask for the ground-floor room. Change the conditions before the cue gets another chance.
breakdown.deepRead:
A lane-alert log curls from a dashboard printer after a weekend of overnight rides. Laleh, the ride-share driver, used to treat the dashboard chime as an annoyance. Then she prints the log and sees the same pattern circled three times: drift near 3 a.m., passenger in the back, chime after a long quiet stretch.

The first warning might have been surprise. The third is evidence. The loop has a cue, a danger, and a next exposure. Laleh does not need a speech about being a better person. She needs to block overnight rides in the app before next weekend.

This is the practical edge of free will. Automatic routines can narrow choice. They can make behavior happen before a person has fully named the pressure. But awareness changes the moral shape of the problem. When the pattern is knowable, the next duty is not just remorse. It is redesign.

A rocketry club makes the same point in a cleaner sequence. The brass arming key hangs from the launch controller. One member keeps skipping the verbal arming call when students crowd the rope line. The safety officer can call him careless and stop there. Or he can treat the skipped call as a foreseeable loop and install a two-voice callout before the key can turn.

Explanation is useful because it points to the lever. Excuse is dangerous when it stops before the lever. Accountability means changing the conditions that let the known loop reach harm again.
breakdown.fullRead:
An orange hold flag sits beside a month-end invoice queue. Saskia, the finance controller, has seen this pressure before: late close, familiar sender name, false vendor domain hidden by speed. The analyst does not mean to approve a fake wire. That is not the question anymore. The shortcut is now predictable enough to design around.

Awareness alone is a weak form of accountability. It can make people feel serious while leaving the next cue untouched. The month-end queue will come back. Familiar sender names will come back. Fatigue, status pressure, and speed will come back. If the only plan is remember to look closely, the known loop still has a clear path to harm.

The stronger move changes the gate. Saskia predicts the next fake invoice will arrive near close, then makes the analyst hover over the vendor domain and place the orange hold flag before approval. The point is not to shame the analyst. It is to make the risky shortcut harder to complete automatically.

A darkroom owner faces the same duty without office screens. Oona knows the late-night routine now: finish a print session after midnight, set the black fixer jug beside the stainless sink, feel too tired to carry it to storage, pour. The first complaint could have been treated as a mistake. After the cue is known, apology is too small. Before printing starts, she chains the jug to a silver recovery can and locks the sink cover.

This is not a broad answer to whether people are free. It is a working answer to what responsibility demands after a loop is visible. If the cue can be predicted and the harm can be named, the next exposure needs containment. A person may not control every automatic impulse in the instant it fires. That does not mean the person has no duty before the next instant arrives.

A glassblowing studio makes the timing plain. Yara, the director, watches her best demonstrator miss one shutoff step when visitors clap. The applause cue is pleasant, public, and repeatable. Treating it as harmless would be negligent once the cold torch valve tag tells the story. She moves the demonstration line behind a shutoff-and-point routine that must happen before anyone bows.

Indira, a closing-shift pharmacy intern, watches the same after-school window. Tearful parents, late refills, the high-risk shelf at eye level, a misread label at 6 p.m. She moves the shelf out of the closing rotation before the next Tuesday rush.

The hard balance is refusing both lazy extremes. Do not use habit as a blank excuse. Do not use blame as if naming fault redesigns anything. The useful middle is specific: name the cue, name the harm, and change access to the next repetition.

Responsibility returns before the next cue. It returns at hotel check-in, in the driver app, beside the arming key, over the vendor domain, before the darkroom session, and at the torch valve. The pattern does not have to be perfect to create duty. It has to be visible enough that doing nothing becomes a choice.

examples.title: Kiran Asks for the Door Wedge

planSpec.domain: diagnosed sleepwalking during hotel travel
planSpec.audience: a person whose sleepwalking has stopped feeling mysterious after two documented hallway incidents
planSpec.stakes: a stranger, staff member, or the traveler could be hurt if the same nighttime loop is treated as unknowable again
planSpec.requiredBeat: At check-in, he looks at the folded sleep-clinic note, feels the old embarrassment, then asks for a door-alarm wedge and ground-floor room because the hallway loop is now foreseeable enough to contain before sleep.

examples.scenario: A folded sleep-clinic note rests beside a hotel key packet at 4:10 p.m. Kiran feels the old embarrassment at the front desk. Two hallway incidents are documented now, and the night loop no longer feels like a mystery. He must decide whether to stay quiet or contain the cue before sleep. He asks for a door-alarm wedge and a ground-floor room before taking the key.
examples.whatToDo: Ask at check-in for the door-alarm wedge and a ground-floor room, using the sleep-clinic note as evidence that the hallway loop is foreseeable.
examples.whyItMatters: The automatic episode may happen during sleep, but the risk is now known while Kiran is awake. Containment belongs before the next night begins.

examples.title: Laleh Blocks the 3 a.m. Rides

planSpec.domain: ride-share driver after repeated lane-drift warnings on overnight shifts
planSpec.audience: a driver who has treated the warning chime as annoying instead of evidence of a predictable loop
planSpec.stakes: a passenger and other drivers share the risk once the drowsy-shift pattern is visible
planSpec.requiredBeat: After printing the lane-alert log, she circles the same 3 a.m. drift pattern and blocks overnight rides in the app before the next weekend, accepting that the known cue now creates a duty to avoid it.

examples.scenario: A lane-alert log curls from a dashboard printer at 9:05 a.m. after Laleh's Saturday shift. She used to slap the dashboard chime silent and keep driving. Now three warnings cluster near 3 a.m. with passengers in the back. In the postmortem, she circles the drift pattern, opens the driver app, and blocks overnight rides before the next weekend.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the lane-alert log as evidence, circle the 3 a.m. pattern, and block overnight rides in the app before the next weekend shift opens.
examples.whyItMatters: The chime stopped being random once the pattern repeated. Known drowsy-driving cues create a duty to avoid the trigger, not merely regret the last drift.

examples.title: Bastien Adds the Second Voice

planSpec.domain: community rocketry club launch-controller arming sequence
planSpec.audience: a volunteer safety officer after a near misfire shows one member always skips the verbal arming call
planSpec.stakes: spectators and students stand behind a rope line that depends on a sequence everyone can verify
planSpec.requiredBeat: The safety officer can call the member careless, but instead holds up the brass arming key, names the skipped call as a foreseeable loop, and installs a two-voice callout before the key can turn.

examples.scenario: A brass arming key hangs from the launch-controller switch while students wait behind the rope line. Bastien, the volunteer safety officer, has just reviewed a near misfire. Noura skips the verbal arming call whenever spectators crowd close. Bastien can call her careless and end the meeting, but he holds up the key and must decide whether to redesign the step. He installs a two-voice callout before the key can turn.
examples.whatToDo: Name the skipped verbal call as a foreseeable loop, then require a two-voice callout at the rope line before anyone turns the brass arming key.
examples.whyItMatters: Blame alone leaves the same crowded cue in place. The second voice changes the arming sequence so the known shortcut cannot pass unnoticed.

examples.title: Saskia Slows the Familiar Sender

planSpec.domain: accounts-payable wire approval after a familiar-sender phishing attempt
planSpec.audience: a finance controller whose team learned that month-end pressure makes one shortcut predictable
planSpec.stakes: a single automatic approval could move six figures before anyone notices the false vendor domain
planSpec.requiredBeat: The controller predicts the next fake invoice will arrive near close, then makes the analyst hover over the vendor domain and place the orange hold flag before approval, turning awareness into a redesigned gate.

examples.scenario: An orange hold flag sits beside the month-end invoice queue at 5:35 p.m. Saskia, the finance controller, predicts the next fake invoice will arrive near close with a familiar sender name. Analyst Beren opens a wire request and starts to approve. Saskia must decide whether awareness is enough. She points to the vendor domain field. The redesign: hover over the domain, place the orange hold flag, then approve only after the check clears.
examples.whatToDo: Make the analyst hover over the vendor domain and place the orange hold flag before wire approval whenever the month-end queue is under pressure.
examples.whyItMatters: The shortcut is predictable at close. The hold flag turns awareness into a gate that interrupts the familiar-sender approval loop before money moves.

examples.title: Oona Chains the Fixer Jug

planSpec.domain: darkroom photographer disposing of chemical fixer after late print sessions
planSpec.audience: a studio owner who now knows fatigue makes the sink-pour routine likely after midnight
planSpec.stakes: hazardous chemical disposal is not excused once the cue, shortcut, and harm are predictable
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before the redesign, the black fixer jug sits beside the sink after late sessions; after the complaint, the owner chains the jug to a silver recovery can and locks the sink cover before printing starts.

examples.scenario: A black fixer jug sits beside a stainless sink at 12:20 a.m. in Oona's darkroom studio. Before the redesign, Oona ends late print sessions tired, sets the jug by the drain, and tells herself she will carry it out later. After the disposal complaint, she changes the room before printing starts: the jug is chained to a silver recovery can, and the sink cover locks before trays fill.
examples.whatToDo: Chain the black fixer jug to the silver recovery can and lock the sink cover before late printing starts, so fatigue cannot reopen the sink-pour routine.
examples.whyItMatters: The risky cue is now known: midnight fatigue plus a jug beside the drain. Changing the room is accountability; another apology would leave the shortcut ready.

examples.title: Yara Moves the Bow Behind Shutoff

planSpec.domain: glassblowing studio torch valve left open during applause breaks
planSpec.audience: a studio director whose best demonstrator keeps missing one shutoff step when the crowd claps
planSpec.stakes: students and visitors are exposed to a known gas risk if the studio treats applause as a harmless distraction
planSpec.requiredBeat: The director taps the cold torch valve tag and says the applause cue is now known, then moves the demonstration line behind a shutoff-and-point routine that must happen before anyone bows.

examples.scenario: A cold torch valve tag dangles beside a cooling glass gather at 2:15 p.m. in the glassblowing studio. Yara taps the tag while Quill, the demonstrator, wipes his gloves. She must decide whether to treat applause as harmless. "The applause cue is known now," she says. Quill says he only missed it when the crowd stood up. Yara points to the demo line. "Then the bow moves. Shutoff-and-point first, applause second."
examples.whatToDo: Move the demonstration line behind a shutoff-and-point routine: close the valve, point to the tag, then bow only after the step is visible.
examples.whyItMatters: The applause cue is pleasant but predictable. Once it is known to pull attention away from the valve, the studio has to redesign the bow sequence.

questions.prompt: A baker has twice left an oven door open during the 4 a.m. rush when delivery drivers arrive early. Nobody was hurt, but the hot door opens into a narrow aisle. What is the best response?
choices: Move delivery check-in until after oven loading and add a door-latch check before drivers enter the aisle.
Tell the baker to feel worse about the near misses.
Do nothing because the door opening was automatic under stress.
questions.explanation: The early-driver cue and open-door harm are now foreseeable. Changing check-in and adding a latch check contains the loop; remorse and automatic-action excuses leave the next rush exposed.

questions.prompt: A caregiver forgets to lock a medicine cabinet when a favorite song starts during cleanup. A child almost reaches the bottles. Which plan best handles accountability?
choices: Promise to be more aware when music is playing.
Move the speaker outside cleanup time and add a lock-before-music rule posted on the cabinet.
Blame the song and treat the near miss as unavoidable.
questions.explanation: The song has become a known cue for the skipped lock. Moving the speaker and posting the lock rule redesign the conditions; awareness promises and blaming the cue do not protect the child.

questions.prompt: A bike mechanic keeps skipping the final brake squeeze when friends stop by the repair stand. A customer notices before riding away. What is the weakest response?
choices: Add a red final-squeeze tag that must be removed before pickup.
Tell the mechanic to avoid all friends forever.
Say the skipped check was a habit, so no further change is needed.
questions.explanation: Habit explains the skipped check but does not settle responsibility. A known friend-interruption cue calls for containment, such as a pickup tag. Calling it habit and stopping there is the failure.

questions.prompt: A night nurse silences a pump alert during charting and forgets to restart it. It has happened twice during short-staffed nights. Which question should guide the fix?
choices: How can we prove whether the nurse is a good person?
What containment blocks the known charting-plus-alert loop before the next short-staffed shift?
Can we define free will clearly enough to assign blame?
questions.explanation: The repeated charting cue and silenced alert make the loop foreseeable. The useful question seeks a block before the next exposure; character judgment and abstract debate miss the redesign point.

questions.prompt: A dog walker knows one gate sticks after rain and has twice watched dogs slip through while she texts owners. What action fits known-loop accountability?
choices: Send a sincere apology after each escape.
Tell owners that rain makes gates unpredictable.
Stop texting at that property and clip a rain-gate carabiner before entering the yard.
questions.explanation: The rain, texting, and sticky gate form a known risk path. The carabiner and texting stop contain the cue before another dog escapes; apology or weather explanation leaves the loop open.

questions.prompt: A lab tech says, "I know I rush labels when the centrifuge alarm and lunch bell overlap, but I will try harder." What should the supervisor require?
choices: A changed labeling gate for the overlap, such as alarm pause, second read, and tray hold before lunch.
A written statement that the tech accepts blame.
A discussion about whether automatic behavior is truly chosen.
questions.explanation: The overlap cue is already known, so trying harder is too thin. A pause, second read, and tray hold redesign the risky moment; blame statements and philosophy leave labels exposed.

questions.prompt: A pottery studio owner has learned that students leave the kiln vent closed when cleanup music starts. The room has filled with fumes once. Which response is best?
choices: Ban music forever in every class, even when no kiln is running.
Add a vent-open card that must be clipped to the speaker before cleanup music starts on kiln days.
Tell students the first fume incident was not their fault because music cued the mistake.
questions.explanation: The music cue matters only because it intersects with kiln days. Clipping a vent-open card to the speaker changes the trigger path; broad bans and full excuse both miss the specific loop.

questions.prompt: A cashier repeatedly leaves a cash drawer open when a manager asks questions mid-count. The store has seen the pattern on camera. What is not enough?
choices: Pausing manager questions until the drawer clicks shut.
Adding a mid-count hand signal that blocks interruptions.
Telling the cashier to remember drawer security next time.
questions.explanation: The camera has made the interruption loop visible. Reminder-only accountability keeps the same cue in place; pausing questions or using a hand signal changes the conditions.

questions.prompt: A ferry captain nearly misses a dock line whenever tourists crowd the rail for photos. After the third near miss, what does responsibility require?
choices: A stronger private promise to focus harder.
An announcement that tourists are distracting.
A rail-clear cue and crew confirmation before the docking sequence starts.
questions.explanation: The tourist-photo cue is now foreseeable. Crew confirmation and a rail-clear cue contain the next docking risk; private resolve and blaming tourists do not redesign the moment.

reviewCards.front: A risky loop is now documented. What changes about responsibility?
reviewCards.back: The loop may still be automatic in the moment, but it is no longer unknowable. Responsibility returns as a duty to contain, redesign, or avoid the cue before the next exposure.

reviewCards.front: Why is awareness alone weak after a near miss?
reviewCards.back: Awareness can fade while the cue remains. A stronger response changes access, timing, tools, or checks so the known loop cannot reach harm as easily next time.

reviewCards.front: A habit explanation makes behavior understandable. What must it not become?
reviewCards.back: It must not become a full excuse that stops before redesign. Explanation should point to the lever: cue, harm, containment, and the next condition to change.

reviewCards.front: Why is simple blame too small for a known risky loop?
reviewCards.back: Blame may name fault, but it does not block the next cue. Accountability is practical only when it changes the setup that lets the automatic path repeat.

reviewCards.front: When should someone avoid a trigger entirely instead of adding a reminder?
reviewCards.back: Avoid the trigger when the pattern is repeated, the harm is serious, and a reminder leaves the person inside the same cue under the same pressure.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is moving from explanation to accountable redesign. Name the cue, name the likely harm, and decide whether the right response is containment, changed conditions, or avoiding the cue. The test is whether the next exposure is safer, not whether the person sounds more aware.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a near miss repeats under the same cue, then I will write the cue and harm before discussing blame, and I will choose one condition to change before the next shift.
If I can predict the setting where I lose control, then I will remove access, add a physical block, or avoid that setting before relying on resolve.
If someone explains a mistake as automatic, then I will ask what the explanation tells us to redesign and who owns the change before the next exposure.
If a known cue can hurt another person, then I will treat reminder-only plans as insufficient and require containment or avoidance.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one loop that could harm someone if repeated. Write the cue, the harm, and one containment that will be in place before the cue appears again.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one mistake or near miss. Ask whether the loop is now foreseeable and whether the response changed the next exposure, not just the explanation.

memorableLines.text: Once the loop is visible, you no longer get to call it mysterious.
memorableLines.why: It states the responsibility shift in plain, memorable terms.

memorableLines.text: Explanation is useful because it points to the lever.
memorableLines.why: It separates habit explanation from habit excuse.

memorableLines.text: Responsibility returns before the next cue.
memorableLines.why: It locates accountability before repetition, not after regret.
